messages.subject: Covariates and sample size
parts:
Hi all,

I am using observers as a covariate but one of the observers only have 3
detections. Should I eliminate this observer from my data set? or should
I pool this observer with another observer?
Thank you in adavance.

Manuel Spinola

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Covariates and sample size
parts:
On Tue, 23 Aug 2005 15:57:03 +0100, Manuel Spinola wrote:

> >Hi all,

> >I am using observers as a covariate but one of the observers only have 3
> >detections. Should I eliminate this observer from my data set? or should
> >I pool this observer with another observer?
> >Thank you in adavance.

> >Manuel Spinola

Hi Manuel, list,

I think there's no perfect answer, although I'd be interested to hear if
anyone else feels differently.

If you assigned observers to transects at random then there should be no
bias associated with dropping their effort. Presumably if they saw few
objects then this is only a small part of the total effort, so variance
should not be increased greatly.

Alternatively, you could leave the observer in - you'll probably find that
the covariate value associated with this observer has a large variance,
which is what one would expect. So long as the estimated scale parameter is
not really silly you could be content with this.

Another alternative would be to group your observers into categories
(experienced/inexperienced or some such) and try those.

Lastly, ask yourself why you are using covariates in the first place. If
you are simply interested in an overall estimate of abundance then you may
be better not using observer as a covariate at all, and relying on pooling
robustness to give you an unbiased estimate of abundance. The only reason
to use covariates in this case is to increase precision, and the component
of the variance coming from the detection function is typically small, so
you won't get much gain. If you do want to try covariates then dividing
observers into categories might be as far as you want to go (and then using
AIC to tell you whether this is "better" than no covariates).

If, on the other hand, you are interested in density by region or by year
then a global detection function with no covariates will potentially produce
biased estimates of detection probability by region or year. If you have
different observers in different regions or years, this may have motivated
you to try observer as a covariate. However, an alternative is to try
region or year as the covariate, effectively pooling the observers within
the region or year. Again pooling robustness says you should get an
estimate for each region or year that has little bias (although using region
or year as a covariate is less flexible than full stratification so there
may be some bias). So, if you don't have enough observations from all
observers, you could in this situation try year or region as a covariate
instead and let AIC tell you whether this is "better" than the global CDS
detection function.

As an aside, in this situation (when you want to fit a global detection
function using a covariate but estimate density by stratum) you need to tick
on both the global and stratum boxes in Detection function line of the
Estimate tab in the Model Definition. Look in the online help index under
"Estimating the detection function at multiple levels in MCDS" for more on
this. You probably knew this already, but many people do not!

Hope this helps,

- Len
